title: Make Explicit Connections to Prior Knowledge
author: lstam
summary: The third post in a series on prior-knowledge gaps in a third-grade classroom, this piece addresses the assumption the author admits having held for years: that students will spontaneously connect new content to what they learned in earlier grades without being told to. Citing Sarah Cottinghatt's explanation of Ausubel's meaningful-learning theory and Jamie Clark's warning that 'activating prior knowledge' is not the same as vague reminders or generic starter activities, the piece argues connections must be made explicit, every time, not assumed to transfer just because content was reviewed earlier in the year. The author is candid about a specific mistake from the previous year — assuming students would remember the details of Greek myths (Persephone, Pandora) well enough to build a new Roman myth (Cupid and Psyche) on top of them, when in fact they only recalled a few scant details — and describes the fix: always including a short recap of prior content before building on it, rather than trusting memory. For schools whose curriculum isn't vertically aligned across grades, the piece offers a fallback: connect new content to whatever students are likely already familiar with (local geography, commonly read stories) instead of assuming a prior-grade foundation that may not exist. It closes by tying the whole practice to retrieval-practice research via Natalie Wexler, arguing that writing activities which force students to retrieve prior content repeatedly make that knowledge easier to connect to and retain going forward.
points: Directly names a common teacher assumption as the problem: that students automatically connect new content to prior-grade learning without explicit prompting.
Documents a specific, concrete failure: assuming students remembered enough of the Greek myths Persephone and Pandora to build the new Roman myth Cupid and Psyche on top of them — they didn't.
The fix that followed: always include a short recap of the relevant prior content before connecting it to new material, rather than trusting memory from earlier review.

Offers a fallback for schools with non-aligned curricula: connect new content to whatever students are likely already familiar with locally, rather than assuming a prior-grade foundation that may not exist.
quotes: We can make it more likely that students will assimilate new ideas with relevant existing knowledge . . . by stating explicitly what the connections are when we explain things.

Activating prior knowledge is NOT 'vague reminders' or 'generic starter activities.' Instead, we need to 'actively recall and use relevant knowledge before connecting it to new learning' and then 'explicitly [link] prior knowledge to new content.'

I cannot assume that students will make those connections even though it was reviewed at the beginning of the year or because they learned it last year. Too often I have watched students struggle to 'find' or remember what they have learned, or they have inaccurate or incomplete memories of the learning.

One mistake I made last year was assuming they would remember the details of the Greek myths, but they struggled to recall the stories and only remembered a few scant details. This year I have included a short summary of the story to ensure accurate recall.

The more we try to retrieve an item of information, the more likely we are to be able to retrieve it in the future. That's hugely helpful to learning because, as cognitive scientists have found, it's much easier to acquire new knowledge if we can connect it to knowledge we already have.
